summary: Step finding: a child's reading level in kindergarten to grade 2 is associated with their later state reading test results in grade 3, and grade 3 reading with grade 8 reading. In Philadelphia, spring reading screener scores in kindergarten, grade 1 and grade 2 correlated 0.50, 0.53 and 0.73 with the grade 3 English language arts test, and kindergarten entry scores 0.42.
caveats: Correlations, not program effects: this says early reading level predicts later tests, not that a program which raises early reading will raise later tests. Programs attract already-engaged students. The Philadelphia studies are correlations and descriptive cohort results only. One early study had only 54 children; the long-term study across six data sets found early math predicted later achievement more strongly than early reading.

summary: Step finding, checked and not supported on its own: students reading on grade level by grade 3 graduate at higher rates (national and Chicago studies), but in Chicago grade 3 reading level no longer predicted graduation once grade 8 reading and ninth-grade performance were taken into account.
caveats: The national figures are descriptive, with no adjustment. Grade 3 reading reaches graduation only through later reading and ninth-grade performance, which the registry already covers (ninth-grade on track). No Philadelphia study of grade 3 reading and graduation was found.

summary: Step finding: fewer suspensions are associated with less dropping out and more on-time graduation. Middle schools that suspend more raised dropout by 1.7 percentage points in Charlotte (school boundary change) and lowered on-time graduation by about 2 points in North Carolina; in Florida each added ninth-grade suspension cut the odds of graduating by 20 percent.
caveats: The strongest studies compare stricter and less strict schools or principals, not programs that reduce a student's suspensions. The North Carolina graduation result is only marginally significant, and the Charlotte study is a working paper. The Florida study adjusts for attendance and course performance but not earlier test scores. The meta-analysis pools mostly correlational studies. See EP-05: Philadelphia's own 2012-13 cut in suspensions brought no achievement gain.

summary: Step finding: being suspended is associated with lower math and reading test scores. A Philadelphia study following the same students over time found a suspension lowered the suspended student's math and reading achievement; a meta-analysis and studies in New York City, Arkansas and elsewhere found the same direction.
caveats: Effects on test scores are small or absent in the stronger designs: the Charlotte study found no achievement effect and the North Carolina study about 0.02 standard deviations. The Arkansas authors say the link may come from which students get suspended. See EP-05: Philadelphia's 2012-13 policy change did not raise achievement.

summary: Step finding, checked and not supported: when Philadelphia cut suspensions for minor conduct in 2012-13, students with an earlier conduct suspension had 1.45 fewer absences but no change in achievement, and across the District truancy rose and math and English language arts achievement fell.
caveats: A District policy change, not a partner program. The student-level estimates are described by the authors as associational, and schools did not all follow the policy. Shown beside EP-03 and EP-04 so the null appears next to the associations.
